solutions.latex:
The period of $y=\cot(nx)$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{n}$.

With $n=3$, the period is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$\therefore A$

Replacing $x$ by $4x$ compresses the graph horizontally.

$y=f(4x)$ is a horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{4}$.

$\therefore B$

$\log(x-1)$ is defined only for $x>1$ and $\log(x-1)\to-\infty$ as $x\to1^+$, so $x=1$ is a vertical asymptote.

The log graph has no horizontal asymptote (it increases without bound).

$\therefore B$

Need $x^2-4>0$ (square root defined and denominator non-zero).

$x<-2$ or $x>2$, i.e. $(-\infty,-2)\cup(2,\infty)$.

$\therefore D$

$f(x)=-(x+1)^2-2$, so the maximum is $-2$ at $x=-1\in(-2,1]$.

$f(1)=-6$ is the minimum on the interval; $f(-2)=-3$ is excluded but $-3$ is still reached at $x=0$.

Range is $[-6,-2]$.

$\therefore B$

$f'(x)<0$ where the graph is decreasing, between the turning points at $x=-2$ and $x=2$.

At the turning points $f'(x)=0$, so the endpoints are excluded: $-2<x<2$.

$\therefore B$

Roots of opposite sign require the product of roots to be negative (this also guarantees two real roots):

$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\beta=4k^2-\dfrac{9}{4}&<0\\k^2&<\dfrac{9}{16}\\-\dfrac{3}{4}<k&<\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore C$

Probabilities sum to $k^2+3k+k-k^2-4k+1=1$ for every $k$; each must be non-negative, so $k\ge0$ and $-k^2-4k+1\ge0$, i.e. $0\le k\le\sqrt5-2$.

$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-k^2+0+k+2\left(-k^2-4k+1\right)\\&=-3k^2-7k+2\end{aligned}$$

This decreases for $k\ge0$, so the maximum is at $k=0$: $E(X)=2$.

$\therefore C$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=e^x+xe^x\\&=e^x(x+1)\end{aligned}$$

Let $f'(x)=0$

$$\begin{aligned}x&=-1\ \ (e^x\ne0)\\f(-1)&=-\dfrac{1}{e}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&-2&-1&0\\\hline f'(x)&-0.14&0&1\\\hline f(x)&\searrow&-\dfrac{1}{e}&\nearrow\end{array}$$

$$\therefore\left(-1,-\dfrac{1}{e}\right)\ \text{ is a local minimum}$$

$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=e^x+e^x+xe^x\\&=e^x(x+2)\end{aligned}$$

Let $f''(x)=0$

$$\begin{aligned}x&=-2\ \ (e^x\ne0)\\f(-2)&=-\dfrac{2}{e^2}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&-3&-2&0\\\hline f'(x)&-0.05&0&2\\\hline f(x)&\frown&-\dfrac{2}{e^2}&\smile\end{array}$$

$$\therefore\left(-2,-\dfrac{2}{e^2}\right)\ \text{ is a point of inflection}$$

\exfigure{1367_q15_s1}

$$\begin{aligned}2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3&=4\\\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

From the graph in (a), these points are the equivalent of the $\frac{\pi}{3}$ points on a non-transformed cosine graph, i.e.

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3},2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},4\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\dfrac{7\pi}{3},\dfrac{11\pi}{3}\\4t&=\dfrac{25}{3},\dfrac{125}{3},\dfrac{175}{3},\dfrac{275}{3}\\t&=\dfrac{25}{12},\dfrac{125}{12},\dfrac{175}{12},\dfrac{275}{12}\\\therefore\dfrac{25}{12}<t&<\dfrac{125}{12}\ \text{ or }\ \dfrac{175}{12}<t<\dfrac{275}{12}\end{aligned}$$

(Inequalities in $t$ can be read off the graph).

Hence, the ship cannot cross between 0205 hrs to 1025 hrs, and 1435 hrs to 2055 hrs, exclusive at these timing points)

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{e^x}\,dx&=\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}\,dx\\&=\Big[\ln\left|1+e^x\right|\Big]_{-1}^{1}\\&=\ln|1+e|-\ln\left|1+e^{-1}\right|\\&=\ln\left|\dfrac{1+e}{1+\frac{1}{e}}\cdot\dfrac{e}{e}\right|\\&=\ln\left|\dfrac{e(1+e)}{1+e}\right|\\&=\ln e=1\end{aligned}$$

**Alternatively,** manipulate integrand as such:

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}&=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\&=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}-\dfrac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\&=1+\dfrac{-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\end{aligned}$$

and then integrate to obtain $\left(x-\ln\left|1+e^{-x}\right|\right)$ as the primitive.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: obtaining an integrand that is integrable by manipulation of the original integrand; 2: correct primitive and substitution of limits, or equivalent merit; 3: correct answer

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos A}&=\dfrac{1-\cos A}{\frac{1}{2}}\\1-\cos^2A&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\\cos^2A&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\\cos A&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\therefore A&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\ \ (\text{as }A<\pi)\end{aligned}$$

Since $T_1>T_2>T_3$, $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}<1$. If $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$,

$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt3}\approx0.2679<1$$

If $A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$,

$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt3}\approx3.73>1$$

$$A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\ \text{ only}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: recognising a geometric series and subsequently, $\frac{T_3}{T_2}=\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ in terms of the cosine terms; 2: finding $A=\frac{\pi}{6}$ (other potential solutions include $A=\frac{5\pi}{6}$ and also when $\cos A=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$), or equivalent merit; 3: fully correct solution, with due consideration of the possible quadrant for $\angle A$ and also $T_1>T_2>T_3$

solutions.latex:
Since $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$,

$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=1+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\T_2&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\r&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{2+\sqrt3}{2}}=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt3}\\&\approx0.2679\cdots<1\end{aligned}$$

Hence a limiting sum exists.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: utilising the value of $A$ to find a value for the common ratio; 2: fully showing the reason why the series has a limiting sum

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}y^2&=(2m-y)(2n-y)\\y^2&=4mn-2my-2ny+y^2\\2my+2ny&=4mn\\y&=\dfrac{2mn}{m+n}\\\dfrac{1}{y}&=\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}\end{aligned}$$

Inspecting $T_2-T_1$:

$$\begin{aligned}T_2-T_1&=\dfrac{1}{y}-\dfrac{1}{m}\\&=\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}-\dfrac{1}{m}\cdot\dfrac{2n}{2n}\\&=\dfrac{m+n-2n}{2n}\\&=\dfrac{m-n}{2n}\end{aligned}$$

Inspecting $T_3-T_2$:

$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{y}\\&=\dfrac{1}{n}\cdot\dfrac{2m}{2m}-\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}\\&=\dfrac{2m-m-n}{2mn}\\&=\dfrac{m-n}{2mn}=T_2-T_1\end{aligned}$$

As $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$, the three terms form an arithmetic sequence.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: expansion of $y^2$ equation, or equivalent merit; 2: the values of $T_3-T_2$ and $T_2-T_1$ in terms of $y$, $m$ and $n$, or equivalent merit; 3: correct solution. Note that students who automatically assumed $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$ can only receive 2 out of 3 marks maximum, as they assumed the terms were equal prior to showing the terms form an arithmetic sequence
review_reasons: Guide writes T2 − T1 = (m+n−2n)/(2n) = (m−n)/(2n); denominator should be 2mn (final line uses 2mn); transcribed as printed

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle AOT$:

$$\begin{aligned}\cos60^\circ&=\dfrac{AO}{3\sqrt3}\\AO&=\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

From the bearing provided,

$$\angle AOB=270^\circ-240^\circ=30^\circ$$

Applying the cosine rule in $\triangle AOB$:

$$\begin{aligned}10^2&=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2+(OB)^2-2\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right)(OB)\cos30^\circ\\\dfrac{27}{4}+(OB)^2-3\sqrt3\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}(OB)&=100\\(OB)^2-\dfrac{9}{2}(OB)-\dfrac{373}{4}&=0\\4(OB)^2-18(OB)-373&=0\\OB&=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{18^2-4\times4\times(-373)}}{2\times4}\\&=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{6292}}{8}\\&=\dfrac{18\pm22\sqrt{13}}{8}\\&=\dfrac{9\pm11\sqrt{13}}{4}\end{aligned}$$

Since $OB>0$,

$$OB=\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\ \text{metres}$$
